Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Variables
A variable is a name associated with a value stored in memory. The value can belong to any data type and can change while the program is running.
A new variable can be created with an assignment statement:
variable_name = value
For example:
age = 25
name = "Joe"






NoteType hints



Python also allows us to indicate the expected type of a variable using a type hint:
age: int = 25
height: float = 1.82
name: str = "Anna"
is_student: bool = True
A type hint provides information about the intended type, but Python does not enforce it:
age: int = 25
age = "twenty-five"   # Python allows this
In this course, we will normally create variables without type hints:
age = 25
We will return to type hints later when working with functions.



Variable naming rules
Python variable names:

must begin with a letter or an underscore (_);
may contain letters, digits, and underscores;
cannot contain spaces;
are case-sensitive;
cannot be Python keywords.

For example, age, student_age, and _counter are valid names, while 2age and student age are not.






NoteDynamic typing



In Python, the type belongs to the value associated with a variable. A variable can therefore refer to values of different types at different points in a program.


x = 10
print(type(x))

x = "apple"
print(type(x))

x = 4.4
print(type(x))

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Simple data types
In this lesson we use four basic Python data types:



Type
Meaning
Example




int
integer number
25


float
floating-point number
5.5


str
text (string)
"Hello"


bool
Boolean value
True, False




Creating variables
# int
x = 25

# float
y = 5.5

# str
s = "Hello"
t = "World"

# bool
b = True
c = False
Python does not require the type of a variable to be declared explicitly. The type is determined from the assigned value.

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
The type() function
The type() function can be used to determine the type of a value or variable.
x = 25
y = 5.5
s = "Hello"
b = True

print(type(x))
print(type(y))
print(type(s))
print(type(b))
Output:
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'str'>
<class 'bool'>
The type can also change after reassignment:
a = 10
print(type(a))

a = "apple"
print(type(a))

a = 4.4
print(type(a))

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Constants
A constant is a value that is intended not to change while a program is running.
Python has no dedicated syntax that prevents a variable from being changed. Instead, programmers use a naming convention to indicate that a value should be treated as a constant:

use capital letters;
separate words with underscores.

DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 10
MAX_NUMBER_OF_ATTEMPTS = 3






ImportantConvention, not enforcement



Python does not prevent these values from being reassigned. Uppercase names communicate to other programmers that the value is intended to remain constant.


Constants are also often defined in separate modules and imported where they are needed.

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Type conversion
Sometimes a value must be converted from one data type to another. Python supports both explicit and implicit type conversion.

Explicit type conversion
Explicit type conversion, also called type casting, takes place when the programmer deliberately converts a value using a conversion function such as int(), float(), or str().
a = 5
print(type(a))

a = float(a)
print(type(a))
b = 23
print(type(b))

b = int(b)
print(type(b))
c = 10
print(type(c))

c = str(c)
print(type(c))
A conversion is possible only if the value can meaningfully be converted to the requested type.


Implicit type conversion
Implicit type conversion takes place automatically when Python converts a value to another type during an operation.
a = 25
c = 30.0

x = c / a

print(type(a))
print(type(c))
print(type(x))
Here a is an int, c is a float, and the result x is a float.

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Printing variable values
The print() function can display literal text as well as the values stored in variables.
x = 15
y = 20

print(x)
print(y)
Several values can be printed in the same statement:
name = "Joe"
age = 50
is_student = True

print("Name:", name, "Age:", age, "Is_student:", is_student)

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Formatting output

String formatting: format() and f-strings
Python also provides the older format() method for inserting values into strings. You may encounter it in existing Python code, but in this course we will use f-strings for formatted output.


f-strings
An f-string is a string prefixed with f. Variable names and expressions can be placed directly inside {}.
language = "Python"
print(f"{language} is our programming language")
Multiple values can be included in the same f-string:
name = "Joe"
age = 50
is_student = True

print(f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}, Is_student: {is_student}")
Expressions can also be evaluated directly inside an f-string:
x = 5
y = 4
print(f"{x} * {y} = {x * y}")
Values can be formatted using a format specification. For example, .3f displays a floating-point value with three digits after the decimal point:
result = 5 * 5.25
print(f"5 * 5.25 is {result:.3f}")






TipIn this course



Use f-strings when you need to combine text, variable values, or expressions in formatted output. The format() method is mentioned only so that you can recognize it in existing Python code.




Raw strings (r-strings)
A raw string is prefixed with r. Backslashes inside the string are then treated as literal characters instead of introducing escape sequences.
path = r"c:\users\public"
print(path)
Compare the following strings:
print("Today\nis\nWednesday")
print(r"Today\nis\nWednesday")
The first string interprets \n as a newline. The raw string displays the backslash and the letter n literally.

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Reading user input
The input() function allows the user to enter a value while a program is running.
Its optional parameter is displayed as a prompt before the input:
x = input("Name: ")
print(x)
print(type(x))






Warninginput() returns a string



The value returned by input() is always a str. If a numeric value is required, explicit type conversion is usually necessary.


For example:
x = input("Age: ")
print(x)
print(type(x))

y = int(input("Age: "))
print(y)
print(type(y))
A Boolean value can also be produced by comparing the entered text:
answer = input("Are you a student? (yes or no) ")
is_student = answer == "yes"
print(is_student)

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Arithmetic operators
Python provides the following basic arithmetic operators:



Operator
Description
Example
Result




+
addition
10 + 5
15


-
subtraction
20 - 7
13


*
multiplication
4 * 6
24


/
division
12 / 5
2.4


//
floor division
12 // 5
2


%
remainder (modulo)
12 % 5
2


**
exponentiation
2 ** 5
32









NoteDivision and floor division



/ performs division and produces a floating-point result. // performs floor division: the result is rounded down to the next smaller whole number.

title: Working with Simple Data Types
text:
Arithmetic expressions
An arithmetic expression is a combination of numeric values, arithmetic operators, and optionally parentheses.
x = 3 + 2 * 5
print(x)
The result is 13, because multiplication has higher precedence than addition.
When several operators occur in an expression, operator precedence determines the order of evaluation.



Precedence
Operators




1
()


2
**


3
unary +, unary -


4
*, /, //, %


5
+, -



Examples:
x = 3 + 2 * 5
print(x)
y = 2 ** 4 + 3
print(y)
Parentheses can be used to make the intended order explicit:
z = (-5 + 16 ** 0.5) / (2 * 0.5)
print(z)






TipUse parentheses for clarity



Even when parentheses are not strictly required, they can make a complex expression easier to read and reduce mistakes.

text:
Introduction to programming
A computer program is a sequence of instructions that tells a computer how to perform a particular task.
Computers ultimately execute instructions represented in machine code. Programming languages allow programmers to express algorithms and instructions in a form that is easier for humans to write, read, and maintain.
Programming languages can be classified in several ways. One common distinction is between low-level and high-level programming languages.
High-level programming languages provide abstractions that allow programmers to focus more on solving the problem and less on the technical details of the underlying hardware.

section: Tools used to create and run programs
text:
Tools used to create and run programs
Writing source code is only one part of creating a program. Several tools may be involved in transforming source code into a program that can be executed by a computer.

Editor
An editor is used to create and modify the source code of a program.
It allows the programmer to write, edit, and save the instructions that make up the program.


Compiler
A compiler translates source code into another representation, usually machine code or object code, before the program is executed.
The translation is typically performed for a larger part of the program at once.


Interpreter
An interpreter executes a program with the help of another program rather than producing a complete standalone machine-code program before execution.
Python uses an interpreter.


Linker
A linker combines separately translated program modules and libraries into the form required to create an executable program.


Loader
A loader loads the executable program into memory so that the operating system can start its execution.

text:
Your first Python program
Traditionally, the first program written when learning a programming language displays the text Hello World.

print("Hello World")

The statement calls the Python print() function.
The text between quotation marks is passed to the function and displayed as output.
Both single and double quotation marks can be used:

print("Hello World")
print('Hello World')

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
Errors in programs
Making mistakes is a normal part of programming. Finding and correcting errors is an important programming skill.
There are several common types of errors.

Syntax errors
A syntax error occurs when the source code violates the grammatical rules of the programming language.
For example:
print("Hello World)
Python cannot execute this statement because the closing quotation mark is missing.
A syntax error usually results in an error message.


Runtime errors
A runtime error occurs while the program is being executed.
For example:
print(5 / 0)
The syntax is valid, but division by zero cannot be performed.
Python reports an exception such as:
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero


Logic errors
A logic error occurs when the program can be executed but does not produce the intended result.
For example:

print("5" + "6")

The result is:
56
rather than:
11
Logic errors can be especially difficult to find because the program may run without displaying an error message.

text:
The print() function
The print() function is used to display one or more values.

Printing a single value

print("Hello")



Printing multiple values
Several values can be passed to the print() function:

print("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday")

By default, Python separates the values with spaces.
Text, numbers, and expressions can also be combined:

print("5 * 6 is", 5 * 6)



Printing an empty line
Calling print() without an argument produces an empty line:

print("First line")
print()
print("Third line")

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
The sep argument
The optional sep argument specifies the separator placed between multiple values.
By default, the separator is a single space.

print("One", "Two", "Three")

A different separator can be specified:

print("One", "Two", "Three", sep="-")


print("One", "Two", "Three", sep="|")

An empty string can also be used:

print("One", "Two", "Three", sep="")

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
The end argument
By default, the print() function ends its output with a new line.
The optional end argument can change this behaviour.

print("One", "Two", sep=" ", end=" ")
print("Three")

In this example, the second print() call continues on the same line.

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
Escape sequences
An escape sequence represents a special character inside a string.
Some commonly used escape sequences are:



Escape sequence
Meaning




\n
new line


\t
horizontal tab


\r
carriage return




New line

print("Monday\nTuesday\nWednesday")



Tab

print("Name\tScore")
print("Anna\t85")
print("John\t92")

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
Quotation marks inside strings
Sometimes quotation marks themselves need to appear in the output.
One possibility is to use different quotation marks around the string:

print("My name is 'Alain'")

Another possibility is to use escape characters:

print("My name is \"Alain\"")

Similarly:

print('My name is "Alain"')

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
Multiline strings
Triple quotation marks can be used to create strings that span several lines.

print("""This text
contains
several lines.""")

Both triple double quotation marks and triple single quotation marks can be used.

print('''First line
Second line
Third line''')

title: Introduction to Programming and Python
text:
Unicode characters
Python strings support Unicode characters.
For example:

print("Python \u263A")

Unicode support makes it possible to work with characters from many different languages and symbol sets.
